{{Short description|American mathematician}}
'''David Earl Zitarelli''' (August 12, 1941, [[Chester, Pennsylvania]] – December 3, 2018)<ref name=Inquirer>{{cite news|author=Cook, Bonnie L.|url=https://www.inquirer.com/obituaries/david-zitarelli-temple-professor-emeritus-expert-american-history-math-20181214.html |title=David Zitarelli, 77, Temple professor emeritus and expert in history of math |date=14 December 2018 |newspaper=The Philadelphia Inquirer}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/delcotimes/name/david-zitarelli-obituary?id=12856907 | title=David Zitarelli Obituary (1941 - 2018) - Formerly of Holmes, PA - Delaware County Daily & Sunday Times | website=[[Legacy.com]] }}</ref> was an American mathematician and historian of mathematics, known for his 2-volume work on the history of mathematics (before 1942) in the United States and Canada.<ref name=HistoryMath>{{cite book|author=Zitarelli, David E.|title=A history of mathematics in the United States and Canada|postscript=; 2019–2022, with Della Dumbaugh and Stephen F. Kennedy|location=Providence, Rhode Island|publisher=MAA Press, an imprint of the American Mathematical Society|lccn=2018024243}}<br>{{cite book|title=Volume 1, 1492–1930|isbn=9781470448295 |last1=Zitarelli |first1=David E. |date=21 October 2019 |publisher=American Mathematical Soc. }}<br>{{cite book|title=Volume 2, 1900–1941|isbn=9781470467302|postscript=; pbk |last1=Zitarelli |first1=David E. |last2=Dumbaugh |first2=Della |last3=Kennedy |first3=Stephen F. |date=28 July 2022 |publisher=American Mathematical Society }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|author=Guthery, Scott|date=December 14, 2019|url=https://maa.org/press/maa-reviews/a-history-of-mathematics-in-the-united-states-and-canada-volume-1-1492-1900 |title=review of ''A History of Mathematics in the United States and Canada: Volume 1: 1492-1900''|website=MAA Reviews, Mathematical Association of America }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|author=Ackerberg-Hastings, Amy|date=January 4, 2023|url=https://maa.org/press/maa-reviews/a-history-of-mathematics-in-the-united-states-and-canada-volume-2-1900-1941 |title=review of ''A History of Mathematics in the United States and Canada: Volume 2: 1900-1941''|website=MAA Reviews, Mathematical Association of America }}</ref>

==Biography==
Zitarelli grew up in [[Holmes, Pennsylvania|Holmes]], [[Delaware County, Pennsylvania]]. He graduated in 1959 from [[Ridley High School]]. At [[Temple University]] he graduated in 1963 with a bachelor's degree and in 1965 with a master's degree. He married Anita Paul in 1966. He received his Ph.D. in 1970 from [[Pennsylvania State University]].<ref name=Inquirer/> His Ph.D. thesis ''Subdirectory irreducible finite inverse semigroups'' was supervised by {{ill|Mario Petrich|qid=Q95216666|short=yes}} (1932–2015), famous among mathematicians for his research in [[semigroup]] theory.<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=35837|name=David Earl Zitarelli}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author=Szendei, Mária B.|author2=Silva, Pedro V.|title=A tribute to Mario Petrich|date=23 November 2021|volume=104|pages=1–9|journal=Semigroup Forum|doi=10.1007/s00233-021-10235-5}} [https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.06673 arXiv preprint]</ref> From 1970 to 2012, David Zitarelli was a faculty member in the mathematics department of Temple University. In 2012 he retired as professor emeritus and he and his wife moved to Minnesota. During his first decade at Temple University, he did research on algebraic semigroups.<ref>{{cite web|title=David E. Zitarelli: An Autobiographical Sketch|website=wordpress.com|year=2018|url=https://davidzitarelli.files.wordpress.com/2018/01/autobio2018.pdf}}</ref> In 1977 he was promoted to associate professor and gained tenure.<ref>{{cite journal|title=David E. Zitarelli (1941–2018)|author=Parshall, Karen Hunger|author-link=Karen Parshall|journal=Bulletin of the Canadian Society for the History and Philosophy of Mathematics|date=May 2019|volume=64|pages=12–13|postscript=; last updated on 10/29/2020|url=https://www.cshpm.org/archives/bulletins/64-2019.pdf}}</ref> Beginning in 1984, he collaborated with Raymond F. Coughlin (who joined Temple University's faculty in 1970) on a dozen textbooks (including multiple editions). Zitarelli later collaborated with David R. Hill (who joined Temple University's faculty in 1973) on the textbook ''Linear Algebra Labs with MATLAB''.<ref name=Inquirer/><ref>{{cite book|author=Hill, David|author2=Zitarelli, David|title=Linear Algebra Labs with MATLAB|year=2003|isbn=0131432745|edition=3rd|publisher=Pearson|postscript=; 336 pages}} (See [[MATLAB]].)</ref> During his 42 years at Temple University, Zitarelli won several teaching awards. He wrote a history, covering the years 1926 to 2000) of the Eastern Pennsylvania and Delaware Section (EPaDel or EPADEL) of the [[Mathematical Association of America]] (MAA).<ref>{{cite book|author=Zitarelli, David E.|title=EPADEL: A semisequiceninial history, 1926–2000|publisher=Raymond-Reese Book Company|date=January 1, 2001|isbn=0964707705|postscript=; 210 pages}} [https://www2.math.upenn.edu/~epadel/history.html EPADEL introduction at math.upenn.edu]</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://sections.maa.org/epadel/history/ |title=EPaDel - Section History |website=EpaDel, MAA Section for Eastern Pennsylvania and Delaware, Mathematical Association of America (maa.org)}}</ref>

In 2004 Zitarelli began working on his comprehensive history of mathematics in the United States and Canada. He completed the first volume, covering the years from 1492 to 1900, in 2018 and was working hard to complete the second volume, covering the years since 1900, when he died suddenly from a heart attack.<ref name=StarTribune>{{cite news|url=https://www.startribune.com/obituaries/detail/0000286972/ |title=Obituary for David Zitarelli |date=December 2018|newspaper=StarTribune|location=Minneapolis}}</ref> The second volume, published in 2021, was completed (up through the year 1941) by [[Della Dumbaugh]] and Stephen F. Kennedy, professor emeritus at [[Carleton College]].<ref name=HistoryMath/> In 2015 the MAA's online journal ''Convergence'' published Zitarelli's article ''Alan Turing in America''.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.4169/convergence20150101 |title=Alan Turing in America |date=2015 |last1=Zitarelli |first1=David |journal=Convergence |doi-broken-date=3 September 2025 |url=https://maa.org/press/periodicals/convergence/alan-turing-in-america|url-access=subscription }} (See [[Alan Turing]].)</ref>

When David Zitarelli died in 2018 after 52 years of marriage, he was survived by his widow, a son, a daughter, and four grandchildren.<ref name=StarTribune/><ref name=Inquirer/>
